title: Format an employee's joining date as "dd-MMM-yyyy" using `DateTimeFormatter`.
shortTitle: Format an employee's joining date as "dd-MMM-yyyy" using DateTimeFormatter

s1_definition.profdef: `DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MMM-yyyy")` builds a reusable, thread-safe formatter, and `localDate.format(formatter)` renders the date as text like "15-Jan-2020". A `Locale` controls the language of the month abbreviation.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya has a date and wants it printed in a friendly format — day, short month name, year. She sets up a stamp with that pattern and presses it on each date.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MMM-yyyy")` builds a reusable, thread-safe formatter, and `localDate.format(formatter)` renders the date as text like "15-Jan-2020". A `Locale` controls the language of the month abbreviation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya has a date and wants it printed in a friendly format — day, short month name, year. She sets up a stamp with that pattern and presses it on each date.

**One line to remember:** `date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MMM-yyyy", Locale.ENGLISH))` prints "15-Jan-2020".

sections.s2_technical:
`DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MMM-yyyy")` defines a pattern where dd is a two-digit day, MMM is a short month name, and yyyy is a four-digit year. Calling `localDate.format(formatter)` produces the formatted string. The three-letter MMM is locale-sensitive, so I pass `Locale.ENGLISH` explicitly to guarantee "Jan" rather than a localised abbreviation that varies by the server's default locale.

DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe, unlike the old `SimpleDateFormat`, so I can declare one as a static final constant and share it across threads safely. The same formatter also parses text back into a date via `LocalDate.parse(text, formatter)`.

The senior nuance is always specifying the Locale for month and day names, because relying on the platform default makes output non-deterministic across environments — a classic production surprise. I reuse a single formatter constant rather than creating one per call, since construction has a cost. Pattern letters are case-sensitive, for example MM is month while mm is minutes, which is a common source of bugs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Statements and reports at the National Bank of India must show joining dates in a human-friendly "dd-MMM-yyyy" format consistently, regardless of which server renders them.

This is exactly what a locale-fixed DateTimeFormatter does — it renders every date the same way everywhere.

The code defines a `DateFormatService` with a shared formatter and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the date 2020-01-15 as a LocalDate.

Step 1: The shared formatter is built once with the pattern dd-MMM-yyyy and English locale.

Step 2: format applies the pattern, rendering the day as 15.

Step 3: MMM renders the month as the English short name Jan, and yyyy renders 2020.

Step 4: The pieces join with hyphens into "15-Jan-2020".

```
INFO: Formatted joining date: 15-Jan-2020
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  LocalDate(2020-01-15)
    │ format(DateTimeFormatter "dd-MMM-yyyy", Locale.ENGLISH)
    │ dd=15, MMM=Jan, yyyy=2020
    ▼
  "15-Jan-2020"
```

```
  2. "15-Jan-2020"
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To render a joining date in a friendly format I build a DateTimeFormatter with the pattern dd-MMM-yyyy, where dd is a two-digit day, MMM is a short month name, and yyyy is a four-digit year, and then call format on the LocalDate to get text like 15-Jan-2020. I always pass Locale dot ENGLISH when the pattern includes month or day names, because MMM is locale-sensitive and relying on the server's default locale makes the output vary between environments.

DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe, unlike the old SimpleDateFormat, so at the National Bank of India I declare one as a static final constant and share it safely across threads and requests, which also avoids the cost of rebuilding it on every call. The same formatter can parse text back into a date as well.

The senior point I stress is twofold: always fix the Locale for deterministic month and day names, which is a classic production surprise when forgotten, and remember that pattern letters are case-sensitive — capital MM means month while lowercase mm means minutes, which is an easy and painful bug. Reusing one well-configured formatter constant gives me consistent, correct dates everywhere statements and reports are generated.
